answer.exemplar: A telescoping sum is one in which most of what one term contributes is undone by the next, so only a thin remainder survives to be evaluated. In the example, the factor 1 over the product of k and k plus 1 splits into 1 over k minus 1 over k plus 1, which is the whole trick: partial fractions turn an awkward product into a difference. Written out, the sum is 1 minus a half, plus a half minus a third, plus a third minus a quarter, and every interior term appears once with each sign, so the partial sums are 1 minus one over n plus 1, which is the number of terms expressed as the value at the last index minus the value at one before it. Two things follow. The interior terms cancel exactly rather than approximately, so the arithmetic stays exact even for large n, and the answer becomes a function of the endpoints alone, which is why a sum of n apparently unrelated fractions can be found without a formula for series. The same pattern handles sums such as 1 over k minus 1 over k plus 1, where the value at the start index is simply kept instead of cancelling.

answer.exemplar: The normal equations come from a demand that the errors cooperate in a particular way. Write the data as the design matrix times the unknowns plus a residual, so the residual measures how far the fitted values miss the data. The sum of the squared lengths of the residual is a function of the unknowns, and the least-squares solution is where that function is smallest. Smallest means every small change leaves it no smaller, which for a smooth function means the directional derivative vanishes in every direction. Working that derivative out, the change produced by nudging the unknowns is the residual dotted with the change in the fitted values, and the change in the fitted values is itself a linear combination of the columns of the design matrix. So vanishing in every direction says the residual is perpendicular to every column, which is written as the transpose of the design matrix times the residual being zero. Multiplying the original equation through by the transpose of the design matrix gives exactly the system the transpose times the design matrix times the unknowns equals the transpose times the data, and the whole content of the system is that orthogonality condition written in coordinates. The benefit is that the system is square and can be solved by elimination, and the price is that it squares the condition number, which makes an ill-conditioned fit worse than solving the underlying optimisation directly.

questions.explanation: Least squares minimises a sum of squares, and the first-order condition for a minimum is that the gradient vanishes, which becomes the statement that the residual is perpendicular to every column of the design matrix. Multiplying the defining equation of the residual through by the transpose of the design matrix turns that geometric condition into a solvable square system. The derivation matters because it shows the normal equations are not a separate trick but the coordinate form of one idea, and it also explains why solving them squares the sensitivity to a badly conditioned data set.

questions.explanation: A rotation has no real eigenvector unless the angle is a whole number of half turns, because turning a real direction always moves it somewhere else. answer.exemplar: Any point in the plane can be written as x times the first coordinate vector plus y times the second, since those two vectors are the standard basis and every vector in the plane is a combination of them. A linear map has to respect both the scalar and the additive part of that combination, so the image of the point x times e1 plus y times e2 is x times the image of e1 plus y times the image of e2. The image of e1 is the first column of the matrix and the image of e2 is the second, so the two columns carry all the information there is and the matrix is nothing more than these two images written side by side. This is why a matrix cannot be built from any two arbitrary images: they must come from a single linear map, which in the plane is equivalent to being a shear-like distortion rather than an arbitrary rearrangement, and in particular the determinant is fixed by the two columns. The practical consequence is that a linear map is fully determined by two input and output pairs rather than by checking the rule on infinitely many points, and the same reasoning in n dimensions shows that n such pairs suffice, which is why an n by n matrix has n squared entries yet only 2n numbers of actual freedom before linearity is imposed.

questions.explanation: Linearity means the map passes combinations through unchanged, so the image of a general point is the same combination of the images of the two basis vectors. The image of the first basis vector is the first column of the matrix and the image of the second is the second column, so the columns record all the information the map contains. That is the justification for finding a matrix by evaluating a map on the basis rather than by tracking a general point, and it shows a map of the plane is fixed by two input and output pairs.
questions.hint: Write a general point as a combination of the two basis vectors and apply the map term by term.

answer.exemplar: The trace and the determinant are summaries of a matrix that do not depend on the choice of basis, and the eigenvalues are what tie those summaries to the geometry of the map. Each eigenvector is a direction the map does not turn, and it is stretched by its own eigenvalue, so the total stretching summed over all the eigen-directions is the trace and the total volume scaling is the determinant. When a matrix has real eigenvalues this is easy to read off: the matrix with rows (4, 2) and (1, 3) has eigenvalues 5 and 2, which add to the trace 7 and multiply to the determinant 10, and the same 7 and 10 appear from the entries of the matrix itself. The value of the statement is that two small numbers describe a great deal of behaviour. A large eigenvalue beside a small one means the map flattens one direction and stretches another, which is exactly the fingerprint of a shear, and if the eigenvalues are a complex conjugate pair no real direction is preserved at all, which is what a rotation does. Neither fact is visible from the entries alone without solving the characteristic equation, so the summaries are a genuine shortcut for reading a matrix.

questions.explanation: Each eigenvalue is the factor by which the map stretches one eigen-direction, so their sum is the trace and their product is the determinant, and both quantities are computable directly from the entries as well. The pair therefore compresses a great deal of behaviour into two numbers, and the shape of the pair is diagnostic: one large with one small means a flattening and a stretching, while a complex conjugate pair means no real direction is preserved. Neither feature is visible from the entries alone without finding the eigenvalues.
questions.hint: Compare the entries of the matrix with the sum and the product of its eigenvalues.

questions.explanation: A recursive rule must be applied once for every term after the first, and the fifth term therefore needs four applications, not one. Applying it once gives 2 times 4 minus 3, that is 5, which is the second term, and the remaining applications give 7, then 11, then 19. Confusing the number of applications with the index is the classic off-by-one in a recursion, and the same error appears in the arithmetic formula, where the first term needs no step. A quick check is that a_n should equal a_1 plus (n - 1) steps, so the count is always one short of the index.
